newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia rebels free troops, boost peace hopes.
newsitem.headline: Colombia rebels free troops, boost peace hopes.

text.p: Leftist rebels ended Latin America's longest-running hostage crisis on Sunday by releasing 70 soldiers and marines they took prisoner months ago.

Mothers and sons wept as they were reunited in the central square under the gaze of some 200 heavily armed guerrillas and thousands of onlookers. The Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) seized 60 soldiers in fighting more than nine months ago and 10 marines in combat last January.
Cmdr. Joaquin Gomez, head of the FARC's so-called Southern Bloc, called at the ceremony for the country to strive for peace with social justice.

Gomez also read a public communique from the FARC's supreme leader, Manuel "Sureshot" Marulanda, which mapped out a series of pre-conditions which the government would have to fulfil if peace talks were to be launched.
Interior Minister Carlos Holmes said he believed the handover could open the door to eventual talks aimed at ending Colombia's 30-year uprising.
But army commander Gen. Manuel Jose Bonett vowed to hunt the rebels down after this part of the southern province of Caqueta was remilitarized on June 23.

Marulanda's communique called for an end to civilian self- defence organisations, known as Convivir. The FARC chief also called for a zone of southern Colombia to be permanently demilitarized as a site for exploratory talks.

The FARC's Aug. 30, 1996, attack on the Las Delicias military base in neighbouring Putumayo province, in which the 60 soldiers were captured and some 30 others were killed, was one of the most humiliating defeats for the army in the long history of Colombia's internal war.

Political analysts said the FARC also scored one of its most important political triumphs by forcing the army to pull out of a 5,000-square-mile (13,000-sq km) jungle zone for 32 days to make way for the troop release. It was the first time the military had ceded such a large area to the rebels.

"This is a spectacular public relations and even diplomatic triumph for the FARC, who will only increase their armed belligerance," Enrique Santos wrote in his Sunday column in the leading newspaper El Tiempo.
But the bishop of nearby San Vicente del Caguan, Augusto Castro, who played a key role in the hostage handover, said there was a ray of hope for an end to the violence.
"This (release) was an aperitif for peace that will open up an appetite for real and long-lasting peace," he said.
Later in the day, Interior Minister Carlos Holmes, talking to troops on their arrival at an army base just outside the neutral area, said: "This event has sown the seeds for peace."
In a news conference just before they were formally handed over to their waiting mothers, the servicemen spoke of their time in captivity.
"The situation wasn't the best; the conditions weren't the best. We accepted that and waited with peace and courage," Pvt. Nelson Nunez said.
Few showed any bitterness toward their rebel captors. "These are ordinary people. They have one ideology; we have another," marine Alexander Sape Sanchez said.
The army considered rescuing the group by force but were unable to find the men, whom guerrillas, according to the soldiers' testimonies, had split up into groups of five.
"I was afraid the army may try to rescue us by force but that something terrible would happen because we were guarded by many rebels," said John Dolman Cardenas, another of the marines.

Some of the soldiers admitted they felt humiliated by their capture but Lt. Fernando Torres said none of the troops surrendered early in the combat at the Las Delicias base and none should be punished for cowardice.
